You can report things people say as well as questions people ask. If you want to report questions in your own words, there are some differences in the sentence structure.
She asked if we could make sure we get some dessert recipes too.
You may use and ask different questions on a daily basis. There are wh-questions and yes/no questions.
If you want to report information or a wh-question, you can simply use the reporting clause with the wh-word.

What is your name? →The teacher asked me what my name was.
Where do you live? →The teacher asked me where I lived.
When do you want to have lunch? → My mother asked me when I wanted to have lunch.
When you are reporting yes/no questions, you need to add if or whether. Remember that only whether can be followed by a to-infinitive.

Fernanda: “Do you want to work at the hospital?”
Fernanda asked whether I wanted to work at the hospital.

Luis: “Will you be at the mall later?”
Luis asked if/whether I would be at the mall later.
Did you notice the word order when you were reporting what people asked? The common word order for reporting with wh- or if/whether-clauses is like that of a statement.

My mother asked me when I wanted to have lunch.
Luis asked if/whether I would be at the mall later.

Who is your favorite singer?
The stranger asked me who my favorite singer was.
OR
The stranger asked me who was my favorite singer.

What are the CDs used for?
My friend asked me what the CDs were used for.
OR
My friend asked me what were the CDs used for.

When do you want to have lunch?
My mother asked me when I wanted to have lunch

Fernanda: “Do you want to work at the hospital?”
Fernanda asked whether I wanted to work at the hospital.

What did you study in university?
She asked what I had studied in university.

Did you like the movie?
She asked if/whether I liked the movie.

Why don't you like the actors?
She asked why I didn't like actors.
What happens to ‘do' in the above examples?
You don't use ‘do' in the wh- or if/whether-clauses. If the question is negative, however, you can use ‘do' in the negative.
She also asked whether she could have honey.
She asked why I was doing it.
She wondered if it was possible to have a cheat day.
You can use the second conditional to talk about events that are unlikely to happen in the future or impossible in the present.
If I could take the whole week off, I would be able to teach you everything I know.
You can use this unlikely conditional with would in the main clause.
If + simple past, … would + base form of verb

Sometimes would is shorted to 'd.
If James didn't smoke , he would be healthier.
If James didn't smoke , he'd be healthier.
You can also use other modals like could or might in the main clause. Could means “would be able to” and might means that something is possible but unlikely to happen.

If I had a printer, I could print all my research papers from home.
I could buy a car if I got a raise.

If I spoke Spanish, I might travel to South America.
He might understand the grammar better if he came to school everyday.

images.text:
Vanessa: Well, this is going to be fun! I'm so happy that I can spend the weekend with you two and share my love of cooking and food. If I could take the whole week off, I would be able to teach you everything I know. I think it's really commendable that you are doing this, Peter. You have to be motivated and dedicated to make this sacrifice. If it were easy, we would all have great eating habits and very healthy diets.
Peter: Amy will be here soon, but we can start flipping through the recipes. She asked if we could make sure we get some dessert recipes too. She's not as strong-willed as I am when it comes to sugar. She also asked whether she could have honey.

Vanessa: There are desserts that don't have any refined sugar or dairy in them. They could use maple syrup or honey for sweetness. Unlike with coffee, you don't have to go cold turkey on sugar.
Peter: Oh, good! I feel more gung ho now.
Vanessa: Is Amy going to do the cleanse too? If she could do it with you, it would make it easier for you to stay on track.
Peter: She asked why I was doing it, and when I explained that I want to change my habits, she got interested. She has a pretty healthy diet, but there are some things that she eats too much of. Just bad habits.

Vanessa: Yeah. It's just a matter of recognizing habits and making some small changes.
Peter: Amy has lots of questions for you though. She wondered if it was possible to have a cheat day, you know, a day when you can eat whatever you want.
Vanessa: Well, if she really needed one, she could have a cheat day. For example, if she were at a birthday party and everyone was having cake, she could have a small piece. It's not good to have cheat days though because they make it more difficult to change habits.
